title: Proteome profiling of cerebrospinal fluid and machine learning reveal biomarkers of two forms of Alzheimer’s disease characterized by increased or not altered levels of tau
projectDescription: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that impairs memory, cognition, behavior, and other cognitive functions. Despite significant advances in understanding its molecular mechanisms, a definitive cure remains elusive. However, some treatments have the potential to slow disease progression if applied before brain damage occurs. Therefore, the identification of reliable biomarkers is critical for early diagnosis of AD and effective intervention. Recent advances in proteomics and the increased accuracy of machine learning algorithms have enhanced biomarker discovery and validation. In this study, we used a newly developed proteomic pipeline to analyse cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to profile the proteome of AD patients, which included two different subgroups based on their CSF levels of tau. Then, machine learning was used to identify proteins that best classified the two subgroups of AD patients compared to non-AD controls. The resulting model, based on few CSF proteins, demonstrated high accuracy in predicting AD and differentiating patients with elevated or normal CSF tau levels. These protein classifiers, detectable in the preclinical stages of AD, were further validated in silico using larger, publicly available proteomic datasets, confirming their potential as early diagnostic tools.
sampleProcessingProtocol: CSF samples were centrifuged at 400 x g for 20 minutes and subsequently stored at -80 °C until analysis. Samples were subjected to FASP using Vivacon Spin 10 kDa (Sartorius, Göttingen, Germany). Briefly, 10 µg of proteins were reduced by the addition of 20 mM dithiothreitol (DTT; Thermo Fischer Scientific, Waltham, US) in 100 mM Tris/HCl, 8 M urea pH 8.5 for 30 minutes at 37 °C. The proteins were then alkylated with 50 mM iodoacetamide (Thermo Fischer Scientific) for 5 minutes at room temperature and washed twice in 100 mM Tris/HCl, 8 M urea pH 8.0 at 14,000 × g for 30 minutes. Next, proteins were digested overnight with 0.2 μg LysC (Promega, Madison, US) in 25 mM Tris/HCl, 2 M urea pH 8.0, followed by digestion with 0.1 μg trypsin (Promega) in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate for 4 hours. The resulting peptides were desalted by STAGE-tips with reverse phase C18 (Supelco Analytical Products, part of Sigma-Aldrich, Bellefonte, US), and eluted in 40 μL of 60% acetonitrile in 0.1% formic acid. The volume was then reduced in a SpeedVac (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and the peptides were resuspended in 20 μL of 0.1% formic acid. Peptide concentration was determined using a NanoDrop microvolume spectrophotometer (Thermo Fischer Scientific), and 350 ng of peptides was applied to LC-MS/MS analysis.
dataProcessingProtocol: A nanoLC system Vanquish Neo UHPLC was coupled online to an Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer, using a 75 µm × 150 mm  DNV PEPMap Neo  (instruments and column from Thermo Fischer Scientific). Peptides were separated using a 19 min binary gradient of water and 100% acetonitrile (solvent B), both containing 0.1% formic acid at variable flow rate (ul/min): 6% in 0.500 min at 650 ul/min, 6-8% in 0.500 min at 600 ul/min, 8-11% in 0.700 min at 520 ul/min, 11-21% B in 9.700 min at 520 ul/min, 21-36% B for 4.800 min at 520 ul/min, 36-55% B in 0.500 min at 520 ul/min, 55-95% in 2.300 min at 650 ul/min. DIA was performed using an MS1 full scan (380 m/z to 980 m/z) followed by 199 sequential DIA windows with a 3 m/z without overlap. Full scans were acquired at a resolution of 240.000, with an automatic gain control (AGC) of 5 x 106, and a maximum injection time of 5 ms. Afterwards,199  isolation windows were scanned at the fixed resolution of Astral detector 80.000, with an AGC of 5 x 104 and the maximum injection time set at 5ms. Scan range (m/z) was set at 100 – 1000 and HCD collision energy set at 25%. Data analysis was performed using the software DIA-NN (version 1.8.1), with a predicted library generated from an in silico digested human Uniprot reference database   UP000005640_9606 downloaded in 24.07.2023, allowing for cuts at K* and R*, two missed cleavages, and a minimum peptide length of six . Maximum number of variable modifications set to 1, N-terminal methionine excision and cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modifications enabled, and methionine oxidation, N-terminal acetylation as variable modifications enabled. Mass accurancy and MS1 accurancy were both set at 0.0 for automatic inference.This library consisted of 20921 protein isoforms, 30958 protein groups, 6036186 precursors in 2850551 elution groups. The false discovery rate for peptide and protein identification was set at 0.01%.
